meaning: The Preserver — the principal Hindu deity who descends as avatāras to sustain cosmic order (from √viṣ, 'to pervade')

phonemes.desc: Labiodental or dental approximant [ʋ] plus short [ɪ] — the prefix of pervasion, the sound that spreads.
Retroflex sibilant [ʂ] plus retroflex nasal cluster [ɳʊ], from the root viṣ- ('to pervade, to work') — the name's active core.

pronunciation.approximation: 'VISH-noo' — the first syllable has a crisp, tongue-tip sh; the second is short and resonant.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: विष्णु (Viṣṇu), from viṣ- / viś- ('to pervade, enter, settle')

kin.label: Vedic
kin.form: In the Ṛgveda a relatively minor solar deity; his three strides make him 'the wide-strider'

kin.label: Later epithets
kin.form: Trivikrama ('three strides'), Nārāyaṇa ('son of the primal waters'), Hari

pronunciation.note: The IAST form Viṣṇu marks the retroflex ṣ and the retroflex nasal ṇ. Etymologically the name means 'All-Pervading.' Devanagari विष्णु is the most common theistic spelling; in Vedic mantras the accent may fall differently depending on grammatical case.

domains.title: The Preserver Who Pervades
domains.subtitle: Preservation, Descent, and the Three Strides
domains.lead: Viṣṇu is the second great power of the Hindu triad, the one who sustains what Brahmā creates and what Śiva will one day dissolve. But preservation is not passivity. It requires constant intervention, which is why Viṣṇu descends again and again as an avatāra — a deliberate crossing-down into history, whenever dharma declines and adharma rises.

cards.name: Preservation
cards.desc: He maintains cosmic order (dharma) across the ages — the Gītā's promise that whenever virtue decays, he will come (Bhagavad Gītā 4.7).

cards.name: The Three Strides
cards.desc: As Trivikrama he measures earth, sky, and heaven in three steps; as Vāmana the dwarf he wins them back from Bali (Ṛgveda 1.154).

cards.name: Avatāras
cards.desc: Fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, and the rest: ten descents, each engineered against a specific form of evil (Purāṇas).

cards.name: Cosmic Sleep
cards.desc: Between cycles he sleeps on Śeṣa, the thousand-hooded serpent, a lotus from his navel bearing Brahmā, the next creator (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1).

symbols.name: Discus (cakra)
symbols.meaning: Sudarśana, the wheel of divine will that cuts through illusion and evil.

symbols.name: Conch (śaṅkha)
symbols.meaning: The primeval sound Oṃ, announcing divine presence and the dissolution of boundaries.

symbols.name: Mace (gadā)
symbols.meaning: The power of knowledge; often identified with Kāmadeva or the force of cosmic law.

symbols.name: Lotus (padma)
symbols.meaning: Purity and the unfolding of creation; Brahmā is born from the lotus rising from Viṣṇu's navel.

symbols.name: Garuda
symbols.meaning: The eagle-king, his mount, symbolizing the Vedas and the swiftness of divine knowledge.

symbols.name: Śeṣa
symbols.meaning: The cosmic serpent upon whom Viṣṇu reclines between universes.

mythology.lead: Viṣṇu's mythology grows from a minor Vedic solar figure into the preserver of the cosmos. Its center is movement: the three strides that measure the worlds, the ten descents that enter history, and the long sleep between universes in which everything begins again. No Hindu god has a richer narrative literature — the two great epics are, at bottom, his autobiography.

myths.title: The Three Strides of the Wide-Strider
myths.text: In the Ṛgveda's hymn to the strides (1.154), Viṣṇu plants three steps and measures the universe: the first covers earth, the second the midspace, and the third — 'where the pious dwell, where the Sun marches in step' — reaches past the reach of birds, past the very gods. 'Wide of stride did Viṣṇu stride out; three times he set down his footstep' (RV 1.154.2–3). In the Vedic dawn this is the sun's arc across the sky, the god who is small enough to stand on earth and vast enough to plant his foot beyond heaven. The image was too potent to stay small: the Brahmanas and Purāṇas spent a thousand years unfolding it into the dwarf Vāmana who asked Bali for three paces of ground. The myth means that measurement is mastery — to pace out a world is to own it, and the universe turns out to be exactly three footsteps wide.

myths.title: Vāmana and the Generous Demon King
myths.text: The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.2.5) tells it with ritual brevity; the Purāṇas make it an epic. The demon king Bali — grandson of Prahlāda, ruler of the three worlds through flawless righteousness — had conquered the gods not by sin but by his charity. Viṣṇu came to his sacrifice as a dwarf brahmin boy and asked for as much ground as he could cover in three strides. Bali's guru Śukra cried warning, but the king had already poured the water of the gift and would not break his word. Vāmana grew — the Purāṇas delight in the colossal Trivikrama filling the sky — covered earth and heaven in two steps, and asked where the third might land. Bali offered his own head, and Viṣṇu set his foot there, pressing the generous asura down into the underworld he is allowed to rule — while Prahlāda's pleas win him the boon of returning each year. The myth means that virtue untempered by discernment is a door for fraud: the one king generous enough to give away everything is exactly the one who must lose it.

myths.title: Narasiṃha, the Man-Lion from the Pillar
myths.text: The tyrant Hiraṇyakaśipu had extorted from Brahmā a boon engineered against every conceivable death: not by man or beast, neither inside nor outside, neither day nor night, neither on earth nor in the sky, by no weapon made or unmade (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.2–3). Armed with this loophole, he demanded worship as God. His own son Prahlāda refused, insisting Viṣṇu was everywhere — even, the boy said, in the pillar of the hall. 'Then let him come from that pillar,' Hiraṇyakaśipu sneered, striking it with his mace. The pillar burst, and out came the man-lion: neither man nor beast, at twilight, in the doorway, on the demon's own lap — and with claws, no weapon — Narasiṃha disemboweled the tyrant while the boy looked on. The gods poured flowers. The myth means that boons breed their own nemesis: a contract written against every weapon is defeated by the one form the contract's language could not exclude — and devotion, not loopholes, is what saves.

myths.title: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk
myths.text: When the gods, diminished by a curse, needed the nectar of immortality (amṛta) that had been lost in the deluge, Viṣṇu proposed the great churn: Mount Mandara as the rod, the serpent-king Vāsuki as the rope, the gods pulling the tail and the demons the head, the mountain pivoted on Viṣṇu's own back as the tortoise Kūrma (Mahābhārata 1.15–17; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9). From the seething ocean rose, one by one, the treasures of the cosmos — the wish-cow, the jewel Kaustubha, the apsarases, the moon, the physician Dhanvantari bearing the amṛta, and first of all a poison, halāhala, so terrible that Śiva drank it to save creation, staining his throat blue. Then Viṣṇu, as the enchantress Mohinī, served the nectar to the gods alone, beheading the demon Rāhu who had slipped into the line. The myth means that cooperation between rivals extracts what neither side can reach alone — and that the referee of the cosmos always ends up holding the cup.

myths.title: The Sleep on the Serpent and the Lotus of Brahmā
myths.text: Between one universe and the next, Viṣṇu withdraws all things into himself and sleeps upon the thousand-hooded serpent Śeṣa, floating on the causal ocean (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8). From his navel sprouts a lotus; on the lotus sits Brahmā, born bewildered, unable to find the lotus's root — until a voice from within instructs him to perform austerity, and only then does he become fit to create. From Brahmā proceed the worlds, the gods, and time itself, while beneath everything the sleeper breathes. The image condenses the whole Vaishnava cosmology into one picture: creation as dreaming, the creator as a flower on a stem, and the preserver as the vast body on whom both rest. The myth means that preservation outranks creation — Brahmā has a beginning, a bewilderment, and a teacher, but the one on the serpent simply is: the cosmos is what happens while Viṣṇu breathes out.

lore.syncretism: Viṣṇu absorbed countless regional deities: Kṛṣṇa of the Yādava cowherds, Rāma of the Ikṣvāku line, Nārāyaṇa of the Vedic waters, and the cosmic Puruṣa of speculative Brahmanism. In South India he merges with Śrī (Lakṣmī) and Bhū (earth) in temple theology; in Bengal, he is the serene Nārāyaṇa beside the fierce Kālī. Sri Lankan Buddhism honors him as the guardian deity Upulvan, identified with Viṣṇu; Jainism honors him as a śalakāpuruṣa of the coming age. Vaishnavism became one of the largest religious communities on earth, spanning philosophical schools from the non-dualist Śaṅkara (who read the Gītā as the highest scripture) to the dualist Madhva and the devotional Gaudīya tradition of Bengal — a single god sheltering arguments that refuse to be reconciled.
lore.culturalLegacy: Viṣṇu's presence is woven into the texture of South Asian civilization. The Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata are national epics, performed in village plays, televised during festivals, and cited in political speech — the Gītā's 'whenever dharma decays, I create myself' (4.7) is India's most quoted line of scripture. The Hare Kṛṣṇa movement carried Gaudīya Vaishnavism to the West; ISKCON temples now stand on every continent. His symbols — the conch, the discus, the tilaka mark — identify millions of devotees, and the ideal of the avatāra, a divine descent to restore justice, has shaped Indian political thought, literature, and popular cinema for a century. In an unstable world, Viṣṇu remains the god who promises to come again.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Viṣṇu teaches that the highest power is not the power that destroys but the power that keeps things going. Maintenance is harder than creation; it requires patience, repetition, and the willingness to return to the same task age after age. Every parent who wakes in the night, every farmer who plants again after a flood, every healer who stays with a patient long after the drama has faded — they are images of Viṣṇu.

His three strides remind us that the cosmos is measured, not random. His avatāras remind us that when order collapses, the sacred does not abandon the world but enters it — small, absurd, unrecognizable: a dwarf asking for three paces. His sleep on the serpent reminds us that endings are also wombs. To call on Viṣṇu is to choose the long work of preservation over the short thrill of annihilation. It is to believe that the world, for all its wounds, is worth saving.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Devanagari form is विष्णु. IAST Viṣṇu marks the retroflex sibilant ṣ and the retroflex nasal ṇ. The name is traditionally derived from the root viś ('to enter, pervade'), though Monier-Williams also notes the root viṣ ('to work, be active'). The semantic core is pervasion: the god who is everywhere.

lore.archaeology: The earliest material evidence of Viṣṇu devotion is the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (Vidisha, c. 110 BCE), whose Garuda capital and Brahmi inscription identify Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador, as a Bhāgavata — proof that Vaishnavism had Greek converts within a century of the Mauryas. Gupta-period monuments give the mythology stone: the Varāha panel at Udayagiri Cave 5 (c. 400 CE) and the Anantaśāyin relief at Deogarh, the earliest great narrative images of the sleeping god. The Changu Narayan temple in Nepal (5th century CE) is among the oldest standing Vaishnava shrines, and medieval sites from Tirupati to Angkor Wat testify to a temple culture that carried Viṣṇu's worship across South and Southeast Asia.
